newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition wary over government reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition wary over government reform bill.

text.p: Kenya's opposition said on Saturday it was deeply suspicious of a government reform and anti-corruption bill aimed at pleasing the IMF after it halted a multi-million dollar aid package.

In another twist in the political and economic turmoil rocking the East African country, local newspapers said powerful Minister in the President's Office John Koech resigned on Friday citing ''frustration''.
Attorney-General Amos Wako published on Friday "The Statute Law (Repeals and Miscellaneous Act) Bill 1997" for debate and approval by parliament.
He also proposed repeal of the Vagrancy Act under which police can detain anyone on suspicion of being a vagabond and to amend various laws ranging from banking to public security.

"They have no intention of levelling the playing field to make the election free and fair," said opposition leader Paul Muite, an activist in the unregistered Safina party, adding the government reforms were insincere.
The bill came as business leaders urged the government to take swift action to halt corruption after an IMF decision to block a $205 million three-year loan.
The tough IMF decision rocked the East African nation where President Daniel arap Moi, 73 and in power since 1978, faces elections later this year. No election date has been set.
One leading investment advisor said he received a stream of calls from foreign investors early on Saturday asking how to repatriate money from Kenya.

"The Kenya government's reaction over the weekend will determine what investors do. Investors are waiting for a statement from the president and his silence is perturbing," said the investment advisor who declined to be identified.
The main airport in the Kenyan capital was hit by a strike over pay on Saturday and international arrivals were being re-routed, airport and industry officials said.

Air traffic controllers at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport started a go-slow at midnight on Friday (2100 GMT) delaying outgoing flights and causing incoming flights to be re-routed, an airport official said.
"The strike is on here, our problem is of course money. We don't have enough money," said an air traffic control official.
Koech said frustration led to his resignation and said he would give further details on Monday, according to the independent Daily Nation newspaper.

No government minister has resigned since opposition leader Kenneth Matiba resigned in December 1998 a rash of other ministers followed suit to join opposition parties in the run-up to 1992 elections, analysts said.
The IMF turned down a request from Kenya for more time to meet IMF concerns about corruption and energy sector reform.

Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said on Friday the government had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF halted crucial aid on Thursday in a row over graft.
The ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) recommended last month repeal of 11 contraversial laws and the establishment before elections of a commission to review the constitution.

The National Convention Executive Council (NCEC), the body co-ordinating reform protests, has called a general strike for August 8. Nine people died on July 7 when police moved against a pro-reform demonstration.
